chains.name: Kick drum
chains.role: Impact, pulse and low-frequency anchor
stages: Input trim
Set a predictable level before processing.
Peak roughly -12 to -6 dBFS is a comfortable tracking/mix starting window; do not chase this number if the source is already healthy.
Input level affects every processor after it. Fix clipping at the source rather than hiding it later.
FL Studio: Mixer fader / Fruity Balance
Avoid normalizing every sample to the same peak. Perceived loudness and transient shape matter more.
Corrective EQ
Remove inaudible rumble and solve boxiness before dynamics.
Use a steep HPF only if subsonic energy is unwanted, often around 20–30 Hz. Sweep 150–500 Hz for boxiness; use narrow cuts sparingly.
Low-frequency junk can consume headroom and trigger a compressor without contributing useful kick tone.
Fruity Parametric EQ 2
Do not automatically high-pass a kick. Its fundamental may sit below 50 Hz.
Transient shaping
Adjust the relationship between the initial hit and the body.
Add a little attack for definition, or reduce sustain when the tail masks the bass. Make small moves.
This shapes the envelope before compression, so the compressor responds to the version of the kick you intend to keep.
Transient Processor / envelope tools
Transient shaping is optional. A good sample may need none.
Compression
Control inconsistent hits or reshape punch.
Try 2:1–4:1, medium attack around 10–30 ms, release around 40–120 ms, and 1–3 dB gain reduction as a starting point.
After envelope shaping, compression can stabilize the hit without undoing the transient design.
Fruity Compressor / Fruity Limiter
If the kick is a consistent one-shot, compression may only add noise or flatten it.
Saturation / clipping
Add harmonics and manage peaks for density.
Try gentle soft clipping or saturation; begin with less than 1–2 dB of peak shaving and level-match.
After dynamics gives you a controlled signal to color. Clipping can also be used earlier as a deliberate sound-design choice.
Fruity Soft Clipper / Waveshaper / Blood Overdrive
Listen for a papery click or loss of low-end definition.
Final tone / level
Fit the kick into the whole arrangement.
Try a broad move around 50–100 Hz for weight or 2–5 kHz for beater; these are listening zones, not boost instructions.
Final EQ is placed late because the right balance depends on the bass, snare and arrangement.
Fruity Parametric EQ 2
Compare against the bass at matched loudness. Solo tone can mislead.

genres.Hip-hop / Trap: Prioritize a stable fundamental and clear transient. Shape the tail so it leaves room for the 808; use clipping only if it improves translation.
genres.EDM / House: Tune the kick to the track when musically useful. Keep its envelope predictable for sidechain timing and low-end phase alignment.
genres.Rock: Preserve acoustic attack and room character. Avoid excessive clipping; use parallel compression for energy if needed.
genres.Jazz / Acoustic: Keep dynamics natural. Use corrective EQ and light compression only when the recording asks for it.

chains.name: Snare drum
chains.role: Backbeat, crack and midrange punctuation
stages: Input trim
Establish a healthy input level.
Leave transient headroom; avoid clipping the channel input.
The source level determines how hard all following processors are driven.
Fruity Balance
Check sample velocity and layered-sample polarity before processing.
Corrective EQ
Remove rumble and find boxiness or ringing.
HPF only as needed, often 70–120 Hz; inspect 250–800 Hz for boxiness and narrow resonances.
Cleanup before compression prevents unwanted frequencies from dominating the detector.
Fruity Parametric EQ 2
Do not scoop all low mids. The snare body often lives there.
Transient shaping
Control stick attack and shell/body sustain.
Increase attack for crack; reduce sustain for a shorter, tighter hit.
Shapes the envelope before compression so the compressor reacts to the intended hit.
Transient Processor
A transient shaper can exaggerate bleed and cymbal spill on live recordings.
Compression
Add consistency, density or punch.
Try 3:1–5:1, attack 10–30 ms, release 50–150 ms, about 2–5 dB GR.
After shaping, it controls the new envelope rather than fighting it.
Fruity Compressor / Fruity Limiter
For more aggression, use parallel compression instead of crushing the main snare.
Saturation / parallel
Add harmonics and sustain without losing the dry transient.
Try subtle tape/console drive, or blend a heavily compressed duplicate quietly.
A parallel path lets you add density while retaining the original transient and dynamics.
Fruity Waveshaper / Soft Clipper / Mixer send
Level-match the parallel return. More loudness can masquerade as better tone.
Final EQ / space
Set crack, body and position in the kit.
Listen around 150–250 Hz for body, 2–6 kHz for crack, and 8–12 kHz for air. Add room/plate on a send.
Tone and space are final decisions made in context with hats, vocals and guitars.
Parametric EQ 2 / Fruity Reeverb 2 send
Use pre-delay to keep the initial hit clear.

genres.Hip-hop: A firm transient with controlled body works well. Parallel compression and saturation can create weight without flattening the dry hit.
genres.Pop: Keep the crack present but smooth. Use dynamic EQ if bright samples become piercing in dense choruses.
genres.Rock / Metal: Blend close and room mics carefully. Parallel compression can add sustain; gate only when bleed is distracting.
genres.Jazz: Preserve ghost notes and natural dynamics. Favor subtle EQ and room tone over heavy processing.

chains.name: Closed hi-hats
chains.role: Subdivision, pulse and high-frequency movement
stages: Gain / velocity
Set the sample level and humanize the pattern.
Vary velocity and timing musically before reaching for compression.
Performance variation is often more convincing than a compressor trying to create it.
Channel volume / velocity
A perfectly even hi-hat pattern can feel stiff.
Corrective EQ
Remove low-mid clutter and identify brittle resonances.
HPF roughly 300–600 Hz if needed; inspect 6–12 kHz for harshness.
Cleanup before dynamic processing stops unnecessary energy from triggering it.
Parametric EQ 2
Do not boost the top end by default; many samples are already bright.
Transient / envelope
Adjust tick, sharpness and tail.
Shorten sustain for a tight pattern; soften attack for a smoother texture.
Envelope shaping before compression makes the detector respond to the desired hit.
Transient Processor / sampler envelope
Shortening a hat can change groove perception, not just tone.
Dynamic EQ / de-ess
Catch only the piercing hits.
Target the actual harsh band, often somewhere in 6–12 kHz; start with 1–3 dB dynamic reduction.
After broad EQ, dynamic control catches occasional peaks without dulling every hit.
Maximus multiband / dynamic EQ plugin
Static high-shelf cuts can make the whole pattern dull.
Saturation
Add subtle density or texture.
Very light tape/console drive; level-match output.
After harshness control so distortion does not exaggerate the problem.
Blood Overdrive (very lightly) / Waveshaper
High-frequency distortion can become brittle quickly.
Pan / automation
Create motion and hierarchy.
Use small pan changes, velocity accents and phrase-level automation.
The output stage is the best place to shape movement once the tone is stable.
Pan automation / Fruity Balance
Check mono and keep essential rhythmic information clear.

genres.Trap: Use velocity, rolls and subtle pan automation for movement. Control brittle upper harmonics rather than simply turning hats down.
genres.House: Consistent groove matters more than extreme brightness. Use short tails and restrained stereo movement.
genres.Rock: Preserve the natural cymbal/hat sound. Avoid over-compression and aggressive saturation.
genres.Lo-fi: Try filtering, gentle saturation and softened transients; keep enough definition for the groove.

chains.name: Open hats & cymbals
chains.role: Energy, accents and high-frequency wash
stages: Gain / trim
Set peak level and preserve transient headroom.
Start with conservative level; cymbal peaks can be much higher than perceived loudness suggests.
Prevents later processors from being driven unintentionally.
Fruity Balance
Check tails against the next snare or vocal phrase.
Corrective EQ
Remove rumble and harsh resonances.
HPF around 200–500 Hz only if useful; inspect 5–10 kHz for bite.
Corrective filtering before dynamics avoids unnecessary detector activity.
Parametric EQ 2
Do not remove all body from acoustic cymbals.
Envelope shaping
Control strike and decay.
Shorten sustain for tight electronic hats; preserve natural decay for acoustic cymbals.
Shaping before dynamics gives predictable decay and peak behavior.
Sampler envelope / transient shaper
A gate can sound unnatural on long cymbal tails.
Dynamic EQ
Catch harsh moments without dulling the whole cymbal.
Find the piercing frequency and reduce only when it jumps out; often 1–3 dB.
After broad cleanup, dynamic EQ reacts only to troublesome moments.
Maximus / dynamic EQ
Listen in the loudest chorus where masking and harshness are most obvious.
Stereo / ambience
Place cymbals and create depth.
Keep overhead image coherent; use subtle room reverb if the source is too dry.
Spatial decisions work best after tone and envelope are under control.
Stereo tools / Reeverb 2 send
Avoid widening phasey samples that collapse in mono.

genres.EDM: Short, controlled tails and deliberate stereo placement help the groove. Sidechain only if the cymbal wash masks the kick or snare.
genres.Rock: Preserve overhead realism and natural stereo perspective.
genres.Pop: Smooth upper mids and use short ambience to blend sample layers.
genres.Ambient: Long tails can become a texture; automate wet level and filtering.

chains.name: Toms
chains.role: Low-mid impact and fills
stages: Gain / phase
Balance toms and check polarity/phase with overheads.
Check phase before EQ; preserve transient headroom.
Phase problems cannot be fixed with a tone boost later.
Mixer polarity / alignment
For multi-mic kits, listen in the full kit rather than solo only.
Corrective EQ
Remove rumble and reduce ringing.
HPF only if needed, often 30–60 Hz; inspect 200–500 Hz for mud.
Low-mid cleanup before compression avoids pumping on resonance.
Parametric EQ 2
A narrow notch may help a ring, but do not carve every tom into a thin click.
Gate / expander
Reduce bleed between hits.
Set threshold just above unwanted bleed; use hold and release that preserve the drum decay.
After cleanup, gating is easier to set and less likely to react to rumble.
Fruity Limiter gate / expander
Automation or clip gain can sound more natural than a hard gate.
Transient / compression
Shape attack and stabilize hits.
Transient attack to taste; compression 3:1–5:1, medium attack, timed release, 2–4 dB GR.
Transient shaping first, compression second, for control without losing impact.
Transient Processor / Fruity Compressor
Do not force identical dynamics on every tom hit.
Tone / saturation
Set body, stick attack and character.
Try 80–150 Hz for body and 3–5 kHz for attack; subtle saturation only if needed.
Final tone decisions depend on kick, bass and overhead balance.
Parametric EQ 2 / Waveshaper
Use automation to keep fills exciting without making every tom equally loud.

genres.Rock: Tighten bleed where necessary and use parallel compression for sustain.
genres.Metal: Precise editing and gating may be useful, but preserve the natural decay of large toms.
genres.Pop: Control low-mid bloom and keep fills balanced with the vocal.
genres.Jazz: Favor phase coherence and natural room decay over gating.

chains.name: Drum bus
chains.role: Cohesion, shared tone and rhythmic glue
stages: Bus gain
Set combined drum level before processing.
Leave headroom; avoid clipping from summed channels.
Bus processing reacts to the combined kit, so establish a sensible input first.
Mixer bus fader
Do not use the bus to fix a badly balanced individual drum.
Broad corrective EQ
Correct only whole-kit imbalances.
Use broad, subtle moves; solve individual kick/snare problems on their tracks.
Tone cleanup before bus compression reduces unwanted energy driving the detector.
Parametric EQ 2
A bus EQ move affects every drum. Be conservative.
Bus compression
Create cohesion and movement.
Try 2:1, attack 10–30 ms, release timed to groove or auto, 1–2 dB GR.
After tonal cleanup, compression can make the kit feel like one performance.
Fruity Compressor / Fruity Limiter
If the groove loses punch, slow attack or reduce gain reduction.
Tape / console color
Add shared harmonic character.
Low drive and output level matched to bypass.
After glue compression gives the whole kit a common color.
Waveshaper / Blood Overdrive / third-party tape
Coloration is optional; avoid stacking several saturators by habit.
Parallel compression
Add density while retaining transients.
Heavily compress a send, then blend quietly until the kit gains sustain.
Parallel routing keeps the dry bus intact while adding a compressed layer.
Fruity Limiter / Fruity Compressor on send
Check phase and level-match the return.
Peak control / metering
Catch occasional peaks and verify headroom.
Use gentle clipping only if intentional; compare peak and loudness before/after.
Final stage catches peaks after tone and dynamics are settled.
Fruity Soft Clipper / Wave Candy
Do not mistake a louder drum bus for a better one.

genres.Hip-hop: Parallel compression, saturation and deliberate clipping can add density. Keep the kick/808 relationship intentional.
genres.Rock: Gentle bus compression can glue close mics and overheads; retain transient energy.
genres.EDM: Peak control and sidechain behavior may be more deliberate. Watch kick transients and low-end headroom.
genres.Jazz: Often minimal bus processing. Let the performance and room create cohesion.

chains.name: Sub bass
chains.role: Fundamental low-frequency foundation
stages: Pitch / phase
Confirm tuning and check phase against the kick.
Verify notes against the song key; check mono and polarity.
Pitch and phase are foundational; EQ cannot repair a mistuned or cancelling sub.
Synth oscillator / tuner / polarity
Check the lowest notes on a spectrum analyzer and on more than one playback system.
Gain / cleanup
Set level and remove unnecessary subsonic energy.
HPF only if needed around 20–30 Hz; avoid removing the actual fundamental.
Cleanup before harmonics and compression protects headroom.
Fruity Balance / Parametric EQ 2
The lowest note may sit near the HPF. Use your ears and analyzer.
Harmonic generation
Create audible upper harmonics for small speakers.
Use subtle saturation or parallel distortion while keeping a clean fundamental.
Before final compression if you want the added harmonics controlled together.
Waveshaper / Blood Overdrive / Maximus
Blend distorted harmonics rather than destroying the sine-like core.
Compression
Stabilize note-to-note level when needed.
Try 2:1–3:1, medium attack/release and modest 1–3 dB GR.
After saturation makes the full harmonic signal consistent.
Fruity Compressor / Fruity Limiter
A stable synth patch may not need compression.
Kick interaction
Create space only where kick and sub actually overlap.
Use a short sidechain volume dip or dynamic EQ around the competing fundamental; often a few dB is enough.
Late in the chain, because this is a mix relationship rather than a tone defect.
Fruity Limiter sidechain / automation
Avoid pumping unless the genre calls for it.
Mono / meter
Keep the lowest octave stable and verify peaks.
Keep sub content mono; inspect phase correlation and low-end peak behavior.
Final output check ensures translation and compatibility.
Wave Candy / stereo tools
Stereo width below the low mids can vanish or cause playback inconsistency.

genres.Trap: A stable sine-like core with carefully added harmonics can translate. Tune kick/sub overlap and use short sidechain dips if necessary.
genres.EDM: Precise envelope and kick ducking are common. Time release to the groove rather than choosing a random fast setting.
genres.Pop: Keep low end consistent and avoid excessive harmonic grit.
genres.Ambient: Long, slow movement can work, but maintain a stable fundamental and check headroom.

chains.name: 808 bass
chains.role: Sub weight, melodic bass line and rhythmic impact
stages: Tune / envelope
Tune the sample and shape pitch/decay behavior.
Confirm root note and pitch envelope; check slides/portamento and tail length.
A tuned source avoids downstream EQ and saturation emphasizing the wrong notes.
Sampler pitch / tuner
Check every note and slide, not only the first hit.
Gain / trim
Set level before processing.
Keep headroom for saturation and clipping stages.
Input level determines how hard distortion responds.
Fruity Balance
Avoid hitting every plugin at maximum input just because it sounds louder.
Corrective EQ
Remove unwanted rumble and control low-mid buildup.
Inspect 20–35 Hz for unnecessary energy and 150–400 Hz for mud.
Before saturation, so unwanted bands do not become harmonically louder.
Parametric EQ 2
Do not high-pass the fundamental away.
Saturation / distortion
Generate upper harmonics so the 808 reads on small speakers.
Try soft clip, waveshaping or parallel distortion; blend to taste.
Before final peak control so the added harmonics are included in the final envelope.
Fruity Soft Clipper / Waveshaper / Blood Overdrive
Use a clean parallel layer if distortion destroys pitch clarity.
Envelope / compression
Control note sustain and variation.
Often unnecessary for consistent one-shots; if needed, 2:1–3:1 with modest GR.
After tone creation to control the processed signal.
Fruity Compressor / sampler envelope
Volume envelope automation may be cleaner than compression.
Clip / kick relationship
Control peaks and make space for the kick.
Start with gentle 1–2 dB peak shaving; sidechain or automate only the overlapping region.
Clip after shaping; kick interaction is a final arrangement-level decision.
Soft Clipper / Fruity Limiter sidechain
Do not clip so hard that different notes lose their musical identity.

genres.Trap: Slides, saturation and clipping are common. Keep the fundamental recognizable and manage kick overlap intentionally.
genres.Drill: Pay attention to glide timing and note transitions. Use controlled distortion to retain articulation.
genres.EDM: A clean sub core and tempo-aware ducking may work better than heavy clipping.
genres.Pop: Shorten tails where needed and control note-to-note consistency.

chains.name: Electric bass guitar
chains.role: Groove, low-end support and midrange definition
stages: DI / amp blend
Balance clean DI with amp or modeled tone.
Check phase before blending; DI provides definition, amp adds character.
Source blending and phase should be solved before EQ and compression.
Fruity Stereo Shaper / polarity tools
Flip polarity and compare; time alignment is not automatically better.
Corrective EQ
Remove rumble and reduce muddy buildup.
HPF around 30–45 Hz if needed; inspect 150–350 Hz for mud.
Cleanup before compression avoids low-frequency junk triggering gain reduction.
Parametric EQ 2
The bass fundamental and body vary with tuning and instrument.
Compression
Control note-to-note dynamics and sustain.
Try 3:1–5:1, attack 15–40 ms, release 50–150 ms, 3–5 dB GR as a starting point.
After cleanup to stabilize the performance without compressing rumble.
Fruity Compressor / Fruity Limiter
Use slower attack to preserve pick/finger articulation.
Saturation
Add harmonics and audible midrange.
Subtle tape, tube or amp drive; compare clean and colored versions.
After compression for a consistent signal, or before for more compressor interaction.
Blood Overdrive / Waveshaper
Keep the low fundamental clean if heavy distortion is used.
Tonal EQ
Balance weight, note definition and attack.
Try 60–100 Hz for weight, 700 Hz–1.5 kHz for note identity, 2–4 kHz for pick/finger attack.
After dynamics because compression changes perceived tone.
Parametric EQ 2
Make room for kick and guitars rather than boosting every desirable band.
Kick interaction
Resolve low-frequency masking.
Use a gentle sidechain dip or dynamic EQ only in the overlapping band.
Final because the correct amount depends on the actual kick pattern.
Fruity Limiter sidechain / automation
A small arrangement change can outperform complex processing.

genres.Rock: Amp character and upper-mid note definition are useful; keep compression musical and consistent.
genres.Funk: Preserve transient articulation and dynamics. Avoid over-compressing slap or fingerstyle nuance.
genres.Pop: Controlled low end and stable note levels help the bass translate on small speakers.
genres.Jazz: Use gentler compression and preserve the instrument's natural dynamic range.

chains.name: Acoustic piano
chains.role: Harmony, rhythm and expressive melodic detail
stages: Gain / stereo / phase
Set input and check the recorded stereo image.
Check phase on multi-mic recordings; avoid excessive width.
A phase problem is a source issue, not an EQ issue.
Fruity Balance / Stereo Shaper
Keep the natural left-right perspective consistent with the arrangement.
Corrective EQ
Remove rumble, room buildup and resonances.
HPF roughly 30–80 Hz depending on role; inspect 200–500 Hz for mud.
Cleanup before dynamics prevents room buildup from driving compression.
Parametric EQ 2
If piano is the main harmonic anchor, do not thin it just to make space.
Compression
Control peaks while preserving expression.
Try 2:1–3:1, attack 20–40 ms, release 80–200 ms, 1–3 dB GR.
After cleanup, so the compressor responds to musical notes rather than rumble.
Fruity Compressor
Use automation for isolated loud notes when possible.
Dynamic EQ
Tame hammer attack or resonant notes that jump out.
Inspect 2–5 kHz; use dynamic reduction only on harsh notes.
After broad EQ and compression if those stages expose uneven attacks.
Maximus / third-party dynamic EQ
Do not permanently remove the piano's articulation.
Tonal EQ
Set warmth, definition and air.
Try 1–3 kHz for note definition and 8–12 kHz for air, only if needed.
Late EQ is a contextual finishing move after dynamics.
Parametric EQ 2
Check against vocals and guitars; piano often competes in the same midrange.
Reverb send
Place the piano in a coherent space.
Room or hall; pre-delay roughly 15–40 ms; filter low end from the return.
A send preserves dry attack while letting the reverb sit behind it.
Fruity Reeverb 2 send / Convolver
Longer reverb can blur fast passages.

genres.Pop: Polished clarity, moderate stereo width and controlled ambience.
genres.Jazz / Classical: Preserve dynamics, natural stereo perspective and realistic room/hall sound.
genres.Hip-hop: Filtering, saturation and rhythmic delay can turn piano into a textured loop.
genres.Ambient: Long reverb and modulation can be part of the instrument's identity.

chains.name: Electric piano / Rhodes
chains.role: Warm harmonic texture and rhythmic chord movement
stages: Input / tone source
Set instrument amp, tremolo and pickup tone first.
Choose tine/amp character and input level before corrective processing.
The source's character should be established before mix plugins.
Instrument controls / amp sim
Do not try to EQ a source tone that should be changed at the instrument.
Corrective EQ
Remove low buildup and resonances.
HPF 60–100 Hz if needed; inspect 200–500 Hz for mud.
Before compression and saturation to avoid exaggerating unwanted frequencies.
Parametric EQ 2
Retain warmth if the part is meant to carry the harmony.
Compression
Smooth chord dynamics without removing touch.
Try 2:1–3:1, attack 15–30 ms, release 60–150 ms, 1–3 dB GR.
After cleanup; keep performance dynamics intact.
Fruity Compressor
Use light compression for expressive Rhodes parts.
Saturation
Add tape, tube or amp warmth.
Subtle drive; level-match output.
After dynamics for stable coloration, or before if you want compression to react to saturation.
Blood Overdrive / Waveshaper
Low-mid saturation can make a mix cloudy.
Modulation
Create chorus, tremolo or stereo movement.
Slow chorus with moderate depth; tempo-synced tremolo for rhythmic parts.
After core tone and dynamics so modulation does not confuse corrective processing.
Fruity Chorus / Love Philter
Check mono compatibility, especially on wide chorus patches.
Send FX
Add plate, spring, room or tempo delay.
Filter returns and keep the dry attack clear.
Sends allow the same space to be shared with other keys.
Reeverb 2 / Delay 3 sends
Automate send level between sections.

genres.Neo-soul: Warm saturation, subtle chorus and expressive dynamics; preserve touch and chord detail.
genres.Lo-fi: Tape color, filtering and gentle pitch modulation can create movement.
genres.House: Tremolo and tempo-synced delay can make chords rhythmically active.
genres.Pop: Keep width controlled so the vocal remains centered.

chains.name: Synth bass / Reese
chains.role: Electronic low end with harmonic motion
stages: Oscillator / phase design
Set tuning, phase, unison and envelope at the source.
Keep the fundamental stable; inspect unison phase and mono behavior.
Source architecture determines whether the bass is stable before plugins.
Synth oscillator / phase reset
Random phase can cause note-to-note low-end inconsistency.
Corrective EQ
Remove rumble and excessive low-mid buildup.
HPF only if needed below the fundamental; inspect 150–400 Hz.
Before distortion, so unwanted energy is not amplified into harmonics.
Parametric EQ 2
Do not remove the low end that defines the patch.
Distortion / saturation
Build harmonics and character.
Use tube, waveshaping or multiband distortion; blend parallel layers.
Before multiband control if the distortion needs smoothing.
Waveshaper / Blood Overdrive / Maximus
Parallel distortion retains a stable sub center.
Multiband dynamics
Control low and high bands independently.
Use modest ratios, often 1.5:1–3:1, only on unstable bands.
After harmonic creation so the new spectrum is controlled.
Maximus
Multiband compression can shift tone and punch; use only for a clear problem.
Stereo management
Widen upper harmonics while preserving low center.
Keep sub mono; widen upper harmonics and check mono fold-down.
After tonal and dynamic control, before final send effects.
Stereo Shaper / Chorus
Never assume a wide bass patch will translate in mono.
Sidechain / automation
Make room for kick and create rhythmic movement.
Use a timed volume envelope or a few dB dynamic dip in the overlapping band.
Final mix-interaction stage.
Fruity Limiter sidechain / automation
Use groove-timed release rather than a generic fast setting.

genres.EDM: Sidechain movement is often part of the groove. Keep the fundamental centered and stable.
genres.Synthwave: Chorus and stereo upper harmonics can create width; protect the mono sub.
genres.Industrial: Aggressive distortion and multiband shaping can be stylistic, but preserve note identity.
genres.Pop: Keep width and modulation controlled to protect the vocal and low-end focus.

chains.name: Acoustic guitar
chains.role: Strumming, picking and natural harmonic detail
stages: Source / phase / noise
Check mic placement, DI blend, phase and handling noise.
For multiple mics, compare polarity and timing; record healthy peaks without clipping.
Source quality and phase are more important than corrective plugins.
Fruity Balance / polarity tools
Do not time-align mics automatically; listen for the most natural result.
Corrective EQ
Remove rumble, boom and boxiness.
HPF often 70–120 Hz depending on tuning; inspect 150–400 Hz for boom and 2–5 kHz for pick harshness.
Before compression so low-frequency thumps do not dominate gain reduction.
Parametric EQ 2
The guitar may need its body to blend with bass and vocal.
Compression
Even out strumming and fingerpicking.
Try 2:1–3:1, attack 15–30 ms, release 50–120 ms, 2–4 dB GR.
After cleanup; preserve pick transient and natural movement.
Fruity Compressor
Clip gain can be more transparent than heavy compression.
Dynamic EQ / de-ess
Control pick attack, string squeaks and sharp resonances.
Target 2–5 kHz for pick harshness; locate squeaks by listening rather than assuming a fixed frequency.
After compression if the compressor reveals squeaks or sharp attacks.
Maximus / dynamic EQ
Do not de-ess the entire high end into dullness.
Tonal EQ
Add articulation or air if the part needs it.
Try 3–6 kHz for articulation and 8–12 kHz for air, with broad subtle moves.
After dynamics for final context-aware tone.
Parametric EQ 2
Check in the full arrangement with vocal and cymbals.
Space send
Place the guitar in a believable room or stylized space.
Short room for realism; plate for polish; filtered tempo delay for rhythmic parts.
Sends retain a clear dry center and allow shared ambience.
Reeverb 2 / Delay 3
Too much stereo reverb can blur strumming.

genres.Folk: Natural dynamics, stereo image and room tone are priorities.
genres.Pop: Controlled low end and bright but smooth articulation.
genres.Country: Preserve pick definition and rhythmic precision.
genres.Indie / Shoegaze: Modulation and long reverb can turn strums into a sustained texture.

chains.name: Electric guitar
chains.role: Riffs, chords, melodic lines and texture
stages: Amp / cab tone
Establish the main tone before mix processing.
Choose amp gain, cabinet and mic position; control input level into the amp sim.
Amp/cab tone is the instrument's identity. Mix EQ should refine, not invent it all.
Amp sim / cabinet IR
Avoid stacking amp sims without a deliberate reason.
Noise control
Reduce idle noise while preserving note decay.
Set gate threshold just above noise floor; use release that lets notes ring.
Early noise control prevents hiss from being exaggerated downstream.
Fruity Limiter gate / expander
Automation can sound more natural than a hard gate.
Corrective EQ
Remove unnecessary lows and resonant buildup.
HPF often 70–120 Hz; inspect 200–500 Hz for mud and 2–5 kHz for harshness.
Before compression and modulation to avoid processing unwanted bands.
Parametric EQ 2
Do not automatically scoop 400 Hz; that can make guitars disappear.
Compression
Control dynamics when the performance needs it.
Try 2:1–4:1, attack 10–30 ms, release 50–120 ms, modest GR.
After cleanup; distorted amp tones may already be compressed enough.
Fruity Compressor
Heavy distortion often has little dynamic range left to compress.
Dynamic EQ / resonance
Tame piercing amp peaks without dulling the entire tone.
Find harsh resonances in context, often upper mids; use narrow dynamic cuts sparingly.
After the amp tone is established, because resonances are source-dependent.
Maximus / dynamic EQ
Do not notch-sweep every frequency until the guitar sounds hollow.
Modulation / stereo
Add chorus, phaser, tremolo or layered width.
Use modulation intentionally; check mono and keep a stable center part.
After corrective tone shaping so modulation is not mistaken for a source problem.
Fruity Chorus / Phaser / Stereo Shaper
Double-tracking real performances usually sounds more natural than widening one take.
Delay / reverb send
Create depth, rhythmic repeats or atmosphere.
Tempo-sync delay; filter repeats; short room for placement or long reverb for shoegaze.
Send effects sit behind the dry guitar and can be automated by section.
Delay 3 / Reeverb 2
Long tails need arrangement space.

genres.Rock: Amp and cab tone first; keep post-processing restrained and use double-tracking for width.
genres.Metal: Tight low end, controlled upper-mid harshness and precise performance editing.
genres.Shoegaze: Layer modulation, saturation and long reverb; keep one focused layer to preserve definition.
genres.Pop: Control presence and use short stereo ambience rather than excessive width.

chains.name: Clap
chains.role: Sharp transient and stereo backbeat
stages: Input trim
Set a healthy source level for clap.
Peak roughly -12 to -6 dBFS is a comfortable tracking/mix starting window; do not chase this number if the source is already healthy.
Input level controls every processor that follows; start with headroom.
FL Studio: Mixer fader / Fruity Balance
Avoid normalizing every sample to the same peak. Perceived loudness and transient shape matter more.
Corrective EQ
Remove inaudible rumble and solve boxiness before dynamics.
Use a steep HPF only if subsonic energy is unwanted, often around 20–30 Hz. Sweep 150–500 Hz for boxiness; use narrow cuts sparingly.
Low-frequency junk can consume headroom and trigger a compressor without contributing useful kick tone.
Fruity Parametric EQ 2
Do not automatically high-pass a kick. Its fundamental may sit below 50 Hz.
Transient shaping
Adjust the relationship between the initial hit and the body.
Add a little attack for definition, or reduce sustain when the tail masks the bass. Make small moves.
This shapes the envelope before compression, so the compressor responds to the version of the kick you intend to keep.
Transient Processor / envelope tools
Transient shaping is optional. A good sample may need none.
Compression
Control inconsistent hits or reshape punch.
Try 2:1–4:1, medium attack around 10–30 ms, release around 40–120 ms, and 1–3 dB gain reduction as a starting point.
After envelope shaping, compression can stabilize the hit without undoing the transient design.
Fruity Compressor / Fruity Limiter
If the kick is a consistent one-shot, compression may only add noise or flatten it.
Saturation / clipping
Add harmonics and manage peaks for density.
Try gentle soft clipping or saturation; begin with less than 1–2 dB of peak shaving and level-match.
After dynamics gives you a controlled signal to color. Clipping can also be used earlier as a deliberate sound-design choice.
Fruity Soft Clipper / Waveshaper / Blood Overdrive
Listen for a papery click or loss of low-end definition.
Final tone / level
A clap usually needs less low-mid body than a snare. Layer carefully and check phase.
Try a broad move around 50–100 Hz for weight or 2–5 kHz for beater; these are listening zones, not boost instructions.
Make the final placement decision in the full arrangement, then check mono and level-match.
Fruity Parametric EQ 2
Compare against the bass at matched loudness. Solo tone can mislead.

genres.Hip-hop / Trap: Prioritize a stable fundamental and clear transient. Shape the tail so it leaves room for the 808; use clipping only if it improves translation.
genres.EDM / House: Tune the kick to the track when musically useful. Keep its envelope predictable for sidechain timing and low-end phase alignment.
genres.Rock: Preserve acoustic attack and room character. Avoid excessive clipping; use parallel compression for energy if needed.
genres.Jazz / Acoustic: Keep dynamics natural. Use corrective EQ and light compression only when the recording asks for it.

Set a healthy source level for guitar bus.

Remove rumble, boom and boxiness.

The guitar may need its body to blend with bass and vocal.

Hip-hop / Trap.focus: 808/kick relationship, vocal priority, punchy drums and intentional saturation.
moves: Tune 808s and check every slide against the key.
Use parallel compression or clipping for density, not as a default on every track.
Carve space by arrangement first; keep the lead vocal intelligible.
Use short delays and filtered sends for vocal/ad-lib depth.
Hip-hop / Trap.watch: Low-end masking, over-bright hats, clipped master bus and over-compressed vocals.

Pop.focus: Clear vocal hierarchy, controlled low end, polished transients and consistent section energy.
moves: Automate vocal and instrument levels between sections.
Use dynamic EQ for changing masking rather than permanent deep cuts.
Keep reverbs and delays filtered and tempo-aware.
Use bus processing lightly; make chorus lift through arrangement and automation.
Pop.watch: Too many wide layers, competing midrange hooks and reverb washing out consonants.

Rock.focus: Performance, amp tone, drum impact and believable stereo layering.
moves: Get amp/cab and mic balance right before detailed EQ.
Double-track rhythm guitars with separate performances for width.
Use drum-room/parallel compression to add energy without flattening close mics.
Automate lead guitars and vocal rides.
Rock.watch: Over-scooped guitars, cymbal harshness and bass/kick masking.

Metal.focus: Tight low end, controlled transient peaks, dense guitars and vocal cut.
moves: Edit performances tightly while retaining musical feel.
High-pass guitars only enough to remove unnecessary lows; do not hollow the low mids.
Use dynamic EQ for harsh amp resonances.
Keep kick and bass roles distinct in frequency and envelope.
Metal.watch: Excessive clipping, brittle cymbals, over-gated tails and guitars with no midrange identity.

EDM.focus: Kick/sub relationship, transient precision, automation and intentional sidechain movement.
moves: Design kick and bass as a pair and check phase/tuning.
Time sidechain release to the groove, not a generic preset.
Use automation and filter movement to build/drop energy.
Keep low frequencies centered and check mono.
EDM.watch: Uncontrolled sub peaks, sidechain pumping that fights the groove and wide low-end phase issues.

House.focus: Groove, kick/bass pocket, percussion and evolving repetition.
moves: Prioritize timing and velocity on percussion.
Use sidechain only to create the intended pocket.
Use short rooms, filtered delays and gradual automation.
Keep bass stable and hats bright but not brittle.
House.watch: Overly static loops, long tails masking the next hit and crowded low mids.

R&B / Neo-soul.focus: Warmth, expressive dynamics, pocket and vocal intimacy.
moves: Preserve performance dynamics and use automation for phrase shaping.
Use tasteful saturation on keys/bass and gentle bus compression.
Leave space around vocal consonants and ad-libs.
Use plate/room reverbs and tempo delays with pre-delay.
R&B / Neo-soul.watch: Over-polished timing, excessive top-end boosts and muddy Rhodes/guitar overlap.

Shoegaze.focus: Layered guitars, modulation, sustained ambience and controlled density.
moves: Build layers with different voicings/registers rather than identical copies.
Use sends for long reverb and automate feedback/tails.
Keep a focused midrange anchor among wide layers.
Use filters and volume automation to create movement.
Shoegaze.watch: Everything wide and wet, loss of transient contrast and low-mid reverb buildup.

Ambient.focus: Evolution over time, space, texture and intentional negative space.
moves: Automate parameters slowly across long sections.
Use parallel texture layers and filtered long tails.
Preserve a stable low-frequency anchor if the piece needs one.
Print evolving effects when they become part of the performance.
Ambient.watch: Unintentional clipping from stacked tails and masking from endless sustained layers.

Lo-fi.focus: Texture, constrained bandwidth, gentle instability and intimate dynamics.
moves: Use saturation/noise as an aesthetic layer, not a blanket fix.
Filter intentionally while retaining a clear musical anchor.
Try subtle wow/flutter and softened transients.
Keep drums and bass readable under texture.
Lo-fi.watch: Excessive noise, muddy low mids and harsh digital clipping disguised as warmth.

Orchestral / Cinematic.focus: Dynamic storytelling, articulation, depth and realistic section placement.
moves: Program articulations and expression before mixing.
Use shared hall/stage sends to unify libraries.
Preserve crescendos and automate expression instead of flattening them.
Pan sections deliberately and check depth with pre-delay.
Orchestral / Cinematic.watch: Static MIDI dynamics, too much reverb on every source and frequency crowding in low strings/brass.

plugins: Corrective EQ
Remove a specific problem such as rumble, boxiness or a narrow resonance.
Usually early, before compression if the problem frequency is driving the detector.
Fruity Parametric EQ 2
Do not cut just because a frequency is present. Identify a problem in context.
Tonal EQ
Shape broad warmth, presence, brightness or weight after the source is controlled.
Often later in the chain, after dynamics, for final mix balance.
Fruity Parametric EQ 2
A broad tonal move is not the same as surgical cleanup.
Compressor
Reduce dynamic range, control peaks or shape sustain and punch.
After cleanup; before or after saturation depending on how you want the detector to react.
Fruity Compressor / Fruity Limiter
Attack controls how much transient passes; release controls recovery. Time them to the performance.
Multiband compressor
Control dynamics in selected frequency bands independently.
Usually later, after broad tone shaping, when a specific band is unstable.
Maximus
Not a substitute for good arrangement or corrective EQ. Easy to overuse.
De-esser / dynamic EQ
Reduce sibilance or harsh peaks only when they occur.
After compression if compression reveals more sibilance; before if it is driving the compressor.
Maximus / dynamic EQ plugin
Find the actual harsh band for that voice or source; do not assume one frequency fits all.
Gate / expander
Reduce noise or bleed between wanted events.
Early, after input gain is stable; before heavy compression.
Fruity Limiter gate / expander
Use hold and release to preserve natural tails. Clip gain can be more transparent.
Transient shaper
Change attack and sustain independently.
Often before compression when shaping the envelope that the compressor will react to.
Transient Processor / envelope controls
It is not a compressor. It can exaggerate bleed and noise.
Saturation / tape
Add harmonics, density and non-linear character.
Before compression for the compressor to react to color; after compression for more stable coloration.
Fruity Waveshaper / Blood Overdrive / Soft Clipper
Level-match bypass. Harmonics can increase perceived loudness.
Clipper
Control brief peaks with intentional waveform clipping.
Often late on drum/bass channels or buses, after tone and dynamics.
Fruity Soft Clipper / Waveshaper
Listen for flattened transients, brittle distortion and lost groove.
Limiter
Set a ceiling and control peaks; sometimes used for sound design.
Usually last in a channel/bus chain when peak containment is needed.
Fruity Limiter
A limiter is not a loudness button. Leave mastering headroom when appropriate.
Chorus / modulation
Create pitch/time variation and stereo movement.
After corrective processing; often before send effects.
Fruity Chorus / Phaser / Flanger
Check mono compatibility and avoid widening essential low frequencies.
Delay
Create rhythmic repeats and depth.
Usually on a send or late in an insert chain; filter the feedback path.
Fruity Delay 3
Tempo-sync, filter repeats and automate throws rather than leaving every delay always on.
Reverb
Place a source in a room or create an effect tail.
Usually on a send; filter the return and use pre-delay to preserve attack.
Fruity Reeverb 2 / Convolver
Too much low-mid reverb causes mud. A send gives shared space and easier automation.
Stereo / mid-side
Adjust width and center/side balance.
After tonal/dynamic work, before final ambience if the image needs shaping.
Fruity Stereo Shaper / stereo tools
Check mono fold-down and correlation. Width is not automatically separation.
Sidechain / volume shaper
Create space or rhythmic pumping using a trigger or envelope.
At the point where the mix interaction is most useful, commonly late in the bass/pad chain.
Fruity Limiter sidechain / automation clips
Duck only as much as needed. Release timing determines groove.
troubles: Muddy low end
Kick, bass and low keys overlap; too much subsonic energy or reverb.
Mute layers to identify the conflict; compare kick/bass envelopes; inspect 100–400 Hz.
Choose distinct kick and bass roles; shorten tails; use small dynamic dips only where overlap occurs.
Do not automatically high-pass every track or carve a huge smile-shaped EQ.
Harsh / brittle top end
Stacked bright samples, distortion, resonances or excessive high-shelf boosts.
Listen at low volume; identify whether harshness is constant or only on certain hits/notes.
Use a narrow static cut for a fixed resonance or dynamic EQ for changing peaks; reduce saturation if needed.
Do not solve every harshness issue by turning down the entire instrument.
Weak kick
Poor sample choice, phase cancellation, excessive compression or masking.
Compare kick alone and with bass; check polarity and transient shape; level-match bypass.
Try a better source, adjust phase/timing, reduce competing low end or restore attack.
Do not just boost 60 Hz; the issue may be transient or phase.
Bass disappears on phone speakers
Mostly fundamental/sub with few upper harmonics.
Audition quietly and on small speakers; inspect harmonic content.
Add subtle parallel saturation or a mid-bass layer while keeping the sub stable.
Do not distort the entire low end until the fundamental becomes unstable.
Vocal buried in instruments
Arrangement density and competing midrange, not necessarily a vocal-level problem.
Mute layers, identify parts masking consonants and vocal body.
Rearrange registers, automate competing parts, use small dynamic EQ dips triggered by vocal if needed.
Avoid reflexively boosting vocal presence or crushing the instrumental bus.
Reverb mud
Too much low-mid energy in returns, long decay or too many independent spaces.
Mute sends one at a time; listen to the reverb return solo and in context.
High-pass/low-pass returns, shorten decay, add pre-delay or share a common room.
Do not put a long reverb insert on every track by default.
Flat / lifeless drums
Over-compression, clipped transients, static velocities or poor sample layering.
Bypass bus processing; inspect gain reduction; listen to velocity variation.
Restore attack, automate levels, vary velocity and use parallel compression.
More compression is rarely the first answer.
Narrow / phasey mix
Over-widening, stereo chorus, doubled mono sources or polarity conflicts.
Check mono, correlation and individual wide layers.
Keep core elements centered; reduce side level; use real double-tracking where possible.
Do not use stereo width as a substitute for arrangement.
Mix clips unexpectedly
Summed buses, plugin output gain, parallel returns or excessive pre-master level.
Check meters from source to bus to master; bypass plugins to locate gain jumps.
Reduce source/bus levels and maintain headroom through the routing tree.
Do not fix a clipping master by simply inserting a limiter at the end.
Guitars disappear in dense mix
Too much low-mid masking, over-scooped tone or competing synth/vocal presence.
Listen with bass and vocal; compare rhythm and lead guitar roles.
Restore useful mids, pan double-tracked parts and automate lead phrases.
Do not keep scooping 300–800 Hz by habit.
